613d8e5ea5.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°41′01.23″.
613d8e5ea5.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°41′01.23″, 0°40′56.37″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°06′35.96″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.17, elongation 16°01′12.04″ E). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°47′37.19″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -0.85, elongation 16°04′48.88″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

6161043a17.d:
When Ashwini nakshatra falls on a Tuesday, it is a special yōgaḥ. In the cyclic rotation of time, along with the bad combinations of grahas and nakshatras that indicate the probability of upcoming difficulties, good combinations that grant benefits in multiples also arise. Among such good combinations are the Amrita Siddhi yogas of certain weekdays and nakshatras. They are Sunday-Hasta, Monday-Mrigashirsha, Tuesday-Ashvini, Wednesday-Anuradha, Thursday-Pushya, Friday-Revati, Saturday-Rohini. Good deeds performed on such yogas become especially strong in protecting and nourishing us.
For instance, in Devi Atharvashirsha, it is said bhaumāśvinyāṁ mahādevī-sannidhau japtvā mahāmr̥tyuṁ tarati, that is, one can cross even mahāmr̥tyu by doing parayanam when Tuesday and Ashvini join.
Do upāsanā of Lakshmi Narasimha.

61a9d51422.d:

A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

61d431997a.d:
On this day, peshvA mAdhav rAv waged a war against Raghunathrao, captured him and put him under house arrest at Shaniwar Wada along with his assistant Sakharam Bapu Bokil.

Context: Raghunathrao had marched to the north for expanding the empire, he failed to do so. Instead, he came back to Anandvalli and was again tempted to form an alliance with his generals and fight against Madhavrao. This time, however; Madhavrao was extremely agitated with his uncle's repeated attempts to overthrow him.

622a845462.d: Vṛṣabha-Ravi-Saṅkramaṇa-Viṣṇupadī Punyakala.  For viṣṇupadī-puṇyakāla like vr̥ṣabha-saṅkramaṇa, the 16 ghatikas preceding and succeeding the saṅkramaṇa form a puṇyakāla; in general, the ghatikas closer to the puṇyakāla are even more sacred.
622a845462.s:

---𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍌𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌭𑍇   
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌕𑌰𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌶𑌾𑌤𑌾𑌤𑌪𑌃—

---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌫𑌲𑍇 𑌆𑌹𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌕-𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌃 (𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌃)

62853e773d.d:
On this day, Dhirendranath Datta, the 84-year-old freedom fighter, was arrested along with his son, Dilipkumar Datta, from his residence in the Comilla district by the Pakistan army. The duo was taken to the Mainamati Cantonment where they were tortured to death. Their bodily remains were disposed of in such a manner that they were never found.

Context
Born on November 2 in 1886, Datta fought for India’s independence from British rule. He participated in agitation against the Partition of Bengal (1905), the Non-Cooperation movement (1920-1922) and the Quit India movement (1942-1945). He was arrested several times for his anti-British stance. After the partition (which he opposed), as a parliamentarian, he advocated recognition of bengAli and opposed West Pakistani direct rule.

Operation Searchlight, specially targetting Bengali Hindus and nationalists, began a few days ago. It marked the beginning of the genocide in bangladesh as well as the Bangla war of liberation. Members of the Pakistani military and supporting Islamist militias from Jamaat-e-Islami (lit. Collective of Islamists) killed up to 3 million people, raped between 200k and 400k Bengali women. A further eight to ten million people, mostly Hindus, fled to India.

62a6e1bb85.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°57′45.10″.
62a6e1bb85.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°57′45.10″, 0°57′40.79″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 0°59′14.92″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 2°22′19.61″ W). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 1°57′00.02″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.24, elongation 2°54′24.75″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

634d947a94.d: Umbral magnitude: 1.36 (parimāṇa ≈12.0 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 09:19►02:25 (from 3 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra śatabhiṣak/pūrvaprōṣṭhapadā/uttaraprōṣṭhapadā (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or punarvasuḥ (anujanma) or viśākhā (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: kumbhaḥ, mīnaḥ, karkaṭaḥ, vr̥śchikaḥ get more ashubha phala, mithunam, siṁhaḥ, tulā, makaraḥ somewhat ashubha, mēṣaḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ, kanyā, dhanuḥ shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.

64af5d5004.d:
On this day, a bullet from shivarAm rAjaguru stopped Hassan Nizami's anti-hindu activities (albeit killing an unintended person).

The intended victim
Hassan Nizami (the famous sufi of Chishti order, of Nizamuddin Auliya's known silsilã) was indulging in frenzied anti-hindu activity - including conversions in Central Provinces.  Sita Ram Goel writes:
 
> He published in 1920 a big book, Fãtami Dãwat-i-Islam, in which he advocated all means, fair and foul, by which Hindus were to be converted to Islam. He advised the mullahs to concentrate on Hindu "untouchables", and convert them en masse so that Muslims could achieve parity of population with the Hindus. He disclosed in the introduction to his book that he had consulted many Muslim leaders including the Agha Khan regarding the soundness of his scheme, and that all of them had agreed with the caution that the scheme should be kept a closely guarded secret. Unfortunately for the Khwaja, the scheme came to the notice of Swami Shraddhananda who exposed it, fought it tooth and nail, and frustrated it completely by means of his Shuddhi Movement. 

Even MK Gandhi had objected to his pamphlets (ref. his collected writings). But, Svami shraddhananda was killed by an Islamist.

The attempt
Ganesh Damodar aka Babarao Savarkar had recruited many boys, including rAjaguru to his cause. He had him enrolled in "Amravati Vyaayaam Prasaarak Mandal" which was a gym. This boy was strong by constitution and was an excellent marksman. Archery and shooting were this boy's natural forte. He was summoned by Babarao and was given the task of "eliminating Hussain Nizami". 

Boy was happy at his first assignment. Since he was trained by likes of savarkar, he did all the necessary recce and info-gathering. Boy went to Delhi, studied routine of Nizam, set a trap and waited. Plan was to shoot nizam while his car passed thru a set point. The boy waited and he shot. Flawlessly! Unfortunately, that day it was Nizam's father in law (Somali) who was sitting in usual place where nizam sat.

Codename of Rajguru in this operation was "M" - "M" for Maratha. Veer Savarkar had used same pseudonym to write his "Hindutva" year before.

Aftermath
Hassan, although alive, got the message. Conversions stopped in CP.  
Though consoled by his colleagues Shiv Verma and Chandrashekhara AzAd, it is reported that he always felt guilty at killing the wrong person.

𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
---𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌫𑌲𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌉𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍇  
  
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌫𑌲𑍇 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇---  
𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌃---  
𑌅𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍇 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑌿 𑌚𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌜𑌃---  
𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑍌 𑌚 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌕𑍃𑌦𑍍 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍌 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌵𑍇𑌕𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍 𑌸 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌫𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌮𑍍॥  
  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌯𑌾𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌵𑌲𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌃---  
𑌶𑌤𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌦𑌶𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌕𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌵 𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇 𑌶𑌤𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌶𑌤𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍌 𑌶𑌤𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌤𑌥𑌾॥  
𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍌 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌮𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌾𑌹𑍃𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑍋𑌮𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍇 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌰𑌵𑌿𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍇॥  
𑌅𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍁𑌃।  
  
𑌧𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌵𑌚𑌰𑌿𑌤-𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌯𑌣𑌮𑍍/𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌮𑍍  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌤𑌃 𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌮𑌵𑌾𑌯𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑌾𑌯𑌂 𑌚 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌧𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌮𑌹𑌤𑍍॥௪௮॥  
𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌿𑌨𑍀𑌵𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑍇𑌽𑌥𑌵𑌾।  
𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑍇𑌽𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾॥௪௯॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌯𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌧𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌪𑌦𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌃।  
𑌨𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑌿𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿॥௫௦॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌵𑌤𑍇 ௪-௧௨  
  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍀𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌃।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌬𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍂𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍॥௧௯॥  
𑌅𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌤 𑌏𑌤𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑌸𑌃 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾 𑌨𑍃𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑍋𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌾𑌃।  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍈𑌤𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌮𑍋𑌘𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌷𑌃॥௨௪॥  
𑌏𑌷𑍁 𑌸𑍍‍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑍋 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌨𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌨𑍃𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍇𑌭𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௨௫॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌵𑌤𑍇 ௭-௧௪

6510fa3779.d: Budhaḥ sets into combustion (astamayaH), heading prāk (east), on 2027-Jun-16 01:54. At this moment budhaḥ is at ārdrā-2 mithunam (latitude 2°08′46.04″ S, moving vakra (retrograde)), magnitude +3.64, elongation 11°15′04.15″ E of the Sun. Combustion (mAudhyam) is generally considered to weaken a graha's ability to give full results in its significations; undertakings connected with budhaḥ are traditionally best avoided until it re-emerges.

6519766df3.b: Observed on Śukla-Prathamā tithi of Kārttikaḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
6519766df3.d: Kārttika-māsaḥ begins today --- in the Puṣkara Purāṇa, it is said that during the month of Kārttika, at dusk when the Sun is in Tulā, if one offers a lamp (dīpa) in the sky (i.e., an outdoor or elevated lamp) fueled with sesame oil every evening for the entire month, one attains beauty and great prosperity. As stated by Viṣṇu, one who bathes early in the morning throughout the entire month of Kārttika, who is self-restrained, who performs japa, eats havis, and maintains a disciplined life, is freed from all sins. In the Vāmana Purāṇa, it is said that to please Dāmodara (Viṣṇu), one should donate silver, gold, lamps, gems, pearls, fruits, and the like during Kārttika.
6519766df3.s:
𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌤𑍁𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌿𑌲𑌤𑍈𑌲𑍇𑌨 𑌸𑌾𑌯𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌗𑌮𑍇।  
𑌆𑌕𑌾𑌶𑌦𑍀𑌪𑌂 𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌂 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿॥  
𑌮𑌹𑌤𑍀𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌰𑍂𑌪𑌸𑍌𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌦𑌮𑍍।  
𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌃---  
𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌸𑌕𑌲𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌯𑍀 𑌜𑌿𑌤𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌃।  
𑌜𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌹𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌭𑍁𑌗𑍍𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌾𑌪𑍈𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌮𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌵𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌰𑌜𑌤𑌂 𑌕𑌨𑌕𑌂 𑌦𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌫𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑌮𑍍।  
𑌦𑌾𑌮𑍋𑌦𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌃॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।

651b5afe2a.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śaniḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°33′52.82″.
651b5afe2a.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°33′52.82″, 0°33′42.50″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°40′22.69″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.13, elongation 10°14′15.53″ W). śaniḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°14′15.51″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.70, elongation 10°20′37.67″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

651da2f01f.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in mūlā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°18′37.13″.
651da2f01f.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°18′37.13″, 0°18′29.30″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°00′02.46″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.28, elongation 26°56′19.17″ E). śukraḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°18′39.59″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 26°57′03.50″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

---𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌨𑌾𑌗𑌰𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍋 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌃।  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚॥  
𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌮𑍀 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌪𑌰𑌾।  
𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌾 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀॥  
𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍀 𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍈𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌰𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌹𑌮𑍍।  
𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌯𑍋 𑌹𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌾 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌃॥

6580eb9b6a.b: Event occured on 1245-03-21 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
6580eb9b6a.d:
The army of Gajapati  Narasimhadeva-I, having slaughtered Karimuddin Laghri's unit at Lakhnor, beseiged and won Lakhanuti.

Context: This was the second seige by the gajapati in 14 months. Narasinhadeva had attacked Lakhnauti for 1st time in  around November 1243 and had to tactically retreat till Katashin/Contai in South Bengal in April 1244 before drawing out, ambushing and routing Mamluk forces under Tughan. 659dc5045c.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in pūrvāṣāḍhā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°10′25.98″.
659dc5045c.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°10′25.98″, 0°10′19.16″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°56′02.57″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 0°59′33.62″ E). śukraḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°45′36.59″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 0°49′52.90″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here aṅgārakaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

65aeec4071.b: Event occured on 1678-10-22 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
65aeec4071.d:
Jasvant singh rAthoD of mArvAr died on this day in kAbUl. Excited awrangzeb is said to have exclaimed: “darwaza-e-kufr shikast! shikast!” - door that saved Kafirs, fall! Same year Jazia was imposed all over the empire. Awrangzeb then treid to annex mArvAr and convert its royal infant heir to Islam - only to be foiled by brave durgAdAs.

In a letter written in 1659, Awrangzeb speaks of Maharaja Jaswant Singh as "the infidel who has destroyed mosques and built idol-temples on their sites." Maharaja Jaswant Singh was later suspected by the mogols of covertly aiding shivAjI in his daring raid on shaiste khAn in puNe.

65ce75a311.b: Event occured on 1672-03-26 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
65ce75a311.d: Though their revolt seems to have been sparked off by a relatively insignificant incident, Aurangzeb's persecution of the Hindus was certainly the underlying cause which turned it into a religious uprising. The soldier hit the cultivator with a stick which broke his head, whereupon a body of Satnamis beat the assailant to death. When the news reached the local government administrator, he sent a party of footmen to arrest those men. By then a large number of Satnamis had gathered at the scene. They attacked the footmen, put them to flight and seized their arms. The number of rebels was increasing by the hour. The faujdar of Narnol sent a large body of horsemen and foot soldiers to punish the rebels. But they too were routed by the Satnamis. The movement now spread like wild fire and the number of rebels rose to some five thousand. The Satnamis defeated the faujdar of Narnol, captured the town, demolished a number of mosques and tombs and established their own administration. A belief spread among them that they were immortal and that if one of them was slain, seventy others would spring up in his place! At last, on 16th March 1672, Aurangzeb sent a force of 10,000 horsemen, supported by artillery, under command of Rad-andaz Khan to crush the revolt.

665a12a886.d:
When Revati nakshatra falls on a Friday, it is a special yōgaḥ. In the cyclic rotation of time, along with the bad combinations of grahas and nakshatras that indicate the probability of upcoming difficulties, good combinations that grant benefits in multiples also arise. Among such good combinations are the Amrita Siddhi yogas of certain weekdays and nakshatras. They are Sunday-Hasta, Monday-Mrigashirsha, Tuesday-Ashvini, Wednesday-Anuradha, Thursday-Pushya, Friday-Revati, Saturday-Rohini. Good deeds performed on such yogas become especially strong in protecting and nourishing us.
For instance, in Devi Atharvashirsha, it is said bhaumāśvinyāṁ mahādevī-sannidhau japtvā mahāmr̥tyuṁ tarati, that is, one can cross even mahāmr̥tyu by doing parayanam when Tuesday and Ashvini join.

Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

679c808d01.d:
On this day at 6 AM, 18.5 year old freedom fighter khudIrAm bose, walked firmly and cheerfully to the gallows.

Aftermath
After the hanging, the funeral procession went through the city, with police guards holding back the crowd all along the central artery street. The people kept throwing their flowers on the body as the carriage passed by.

The actions of khudIrAm and Prafulla were defended by many nationalists (including BG Tilak, who was promptly arrested on sedition charges). 

After martyrdom, Khudiram became so popular that weavers of Bengal started weaving a special type of dhoti, with 'Khudiram' written on its side. Boys studying in school colleges wore these dhotis and stitched and walked on the path of independence.

Context
khudIrAm and Prafulla Chaki had tried to assassinate the notorious British judge Douglas Kingsford - but their bomb ended up killing two British women instead.

He had been arrested by constables Fateh Singh, and Shiv prasAd Singh near the Waini railway station (now named after him). On 1 May, he was brought to Muzaffarpur by train - a crowd awaited to see him - he cheerfully cried 'vandE mAtaram'. Narendrakumar Basu had came to Khudiram's defence and mounted a very strong case in his defence (redirecting the main blame to the older prafulla and invalidating khudIrAm's initial statement), but failed.

When he was sentenced to death, his spontaneous reaction was to smile. The judge, surprised, asked Khudiram whether he had understood the meaning of the pronounced sentence. Khudiram replied that he surely had. When the judge asked him again whether he had anything to say, in front of a packed audience, Khudiram replied with the same smile that if he could be given some time, he could teach the judge the skill of bomb-making. Khudiram refused to appeal - but was persuaded to go along by the defence team. 

Influences and early activities
In 1902 and 1903, Sri Aurobindo and Sister Nivedita visited Midnapore. They held a series of public lectures and private session with the existing revolutionary groups for freedom. Khudiram, a teenager, was an active participant in the discussions about the revolution. He joined Anushilan Samiti, and came into contact with the network of Barindra Kumar Ghosh of Calcutta. He became a volunteer at the age of 15, and was arrested for distributing pamphlets against the British rule in India.

67a8a86fb1.d: Vyatīpāta is regarded as the king of yōgas. Though it occurs 13 times every year, the occurrence in dhanurmāsa is special, and this day is special for a number of special observances, such as śivapūjā, pitr̥tarpaṇam etc. One must also give arghyam with the shloka mentioned here, and perform the usual (dhanurmāsa) naivedyam of mudgānnam. Markandeya Rishi has performed upadesham of a year-long vratam, beginning this day, including the pūja of vyatīpata-dēvatā. Puranas also narrate the story of rich merchant names Vishwasakha, who was born as a wild boar owing to denying food to a hungry vipra on Vyatipata day. Having lost half his body to a forest fire, the boar was redeemed from this plight by the Raja Haryashva, who passed by, and gave away his accrued merits from vyatīpāta-snāna-dānam. As a result of this, the wild boar attained a divine form.
67a8a86fb1.s:
𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌬𑌾𑌹𑍋 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌣𑌾𑌶𑌨।  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌬𑌾𑌹𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍍 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌨𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
  
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌫𑌲𑍇 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇  
𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌃---  
𑌅𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍇 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑌿 𑌚𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌜𑌃---  
𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑍌 𑌚 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌕𑍃𑌦𑍍 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍌 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌵𑍇𑌕𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍 𑌸 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌫𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌮𑍍॥  
  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌯𑌾𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌵𑌲𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌃---  
𑌶𑌤𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌦𑌶𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌕𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌵 𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇 𑌶𑌤𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌶𑌤𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍌 𑌶𑌤𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌤𑌥𑌾॥  
𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍌 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌮𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌾𑌹𑍃𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑍋𑌮𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍇 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌰𑌵𑌿𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍇॥  
𑌅𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍁𑌃।  
  
𑌧𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌵𑌚𑌰𑌿𑌤-𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌯𑌣𑌮𑍍/𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌮𑍍  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌤𑌃 𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌮𑌵𑌾𑌯𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑌾𑌯𑌂 𑌚 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌧𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌮𑌹𑌤𑍍॥௪௮॥  
𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌿𑌨𑍀𑌵𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑍇𑌽𑌥𑌵𑌾।  
𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑍇𑌽𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾॥௪௯॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌯𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌧𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌪𑌦𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌃।  
𑌨𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟 𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑌿𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿॥௫௦॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌵𑌤𑍇 ௪-௧௨  
  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍀𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌃।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌬𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍂𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍॥௧௯॥  
𑌅𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌤 𑌏𑌤𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑌸𑌃 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾 𑌨𑍃𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑍋𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌾𑌃।  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍈𑌤𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌮𑍋𑌘𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌷𑌃॥௨௪॥  
𑌏𑌷𑍁 𑌸𑍍‍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑍋 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌨𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌨𑍃𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍇𑌭𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௨௫॥

67b1cf1f57.s:

𑌸𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌪𑌲𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।

𑌅𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍇 𑌭𑍂𑌤𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾 𑌭𑌵॥௧௨௪-௭௮॥  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍀𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌪𑌣𑍈𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌤𑌃।

𑌹𑍋𑌲𑌿𑌕𑌾 𑌰𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍀 𑌚𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌭𑌯𑌦𑌾𑌯𑌿𑌨𑍀।  
𑌤𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌹𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌵𑌂 𑌕𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌗𑍀𑌤𑌮𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌲𑍈𑌃॥௧௨௪-௮௦॥

68200d981a.d: The Rishabha Vahanam festival is also part of the larger Panguni Utsavam at the Sri Kapaleeswarar Temple in Mylapore, Chennai. It celebrates Bhagavan Shiva's ride, the bull Nandi, who is adorned in a special gold-plated vahanam (mount) shaped like a bull. The procession usually begins late at night, around 10:00 PM, and continues until the early hours of morning! The sight of the majestic gold-plated Nandi vahanam, illuminated and decorated with flowers, is a stunning visual spectacle. The procession winds through the Mada streets of Mylapore, accompanied by vibrant music, chanting, and enthusiastic devotees.

683f93adca.b: Observed on Pūrvāṣāḍhā nakshatra of Kumbhaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
683f93adca.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Kari Nayanmar, the 48th of the Nayanmars, hailed from Tirukadavur, and was a learned Tamil scholar. He regularly visited the three Tamil kings, earning a substantial amount of money through his recitations of Tamil Kovais (anthologies). Utilising his earnings, he constructed temples, actively promoting Shaivism. Furthermore, he dedicated himself to serving devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, garnering him Bhagavan's divine grace.
683f93adca.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

685731080d.d:
Swami Lakshmanananda Saraswati and four of his disciples were murdered on 23 August 2008 ( Janmashtami Day) in his kanyA ashram, where he was rescuing and helping tribals who had been converted to Christianity. (A group of thirty to forty armed men surrounded the Ashram. Four of the assailants carried AK-47s and many others had locally made revolvers. Two of the four government provided security guards had gone home to eat, the assailants tied and gagged the two remaining guards.)

Hundreds of people gathered on the route to pay their last respects to Saraswati. Riots erupted when the procession passed through Christian localities. Nativist Kui tribals rose up and fought Maoist and Christian forces. Seven Christian tribals and one Maoist leader were convicted in the case. 

Saraswati received an anonymous threat only a week before his assassination. Ashram authorities also filed a First Information Report (or FIR) with the local police. However, no steps were taken to provide appropriate security cover to him, despite ample evidence that there were very real threats being made on his life and the lives of those he served.

6859935c47.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in ārdrā mithunam, center-to-center separation 0°51′39.62″.
6859935c47.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°51′39.62″, 0°51′16.67″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°03′49.87″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.94, elongation 35°42′58.19″ W). śukraḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°55′29.49″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.96, elongation 35°43′35.47″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

68a236a75c.b: Observed on Rēvatī nakshatra of Dhanuḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
68a236a75c.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

This Nayanmar, a Vellala from Mylapore, was a fervent devotee of Bhagavan Shiva. His devotion transcended the physical forms of worship, as he engaged in profound mental worship. He envisioned constructing temples in his mind, where he performed Manasic (mental) worship. In his inner sanctum, he built the temple of unceasing remembrance, ignited the radiant lamp of self-realization, bathed the divine in the waters of eternal Ananda (bliss), and offered his utmost love as the offering. Through this profound and abstract form of devotion, he achieved salvation.

68fbab6977.s:
𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵𑍇 𑌮𑍇𑌷𑌗𑍇 𑌭𑌾𑌨𑍌 𑌮𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌥 𑌫𑌲𑌦𑍋 𑌭𑌵 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌹𑌨𑍍॥  
  
𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑍇 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌾𑌲𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇---  
𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌪𑍋𑌷𑌿𑌤𑌃।  
𑌪𑌂𑌚𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑍀𑌰 𑌮𑍇𑌷𑌸𑌂𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌣𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾॥௬॥  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑌂 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌯𑌾।  
𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨𑌮𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍍𑌚𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍁𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌮𑍍॥௭॥  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌂 𑌸𑌕𑌲𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌂 𑌮𑍇𑌷𑌸𑌂𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌣𑍇 𑌰𑌵𑍇𑌃।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌯𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨𑌃॥௮॥  
𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌹𑌂𑌤𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌾𑌦𑍇𑌨 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌾𑌤𑍍।  
𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌮𑍇 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌹𑌮𑍍॥௯॥  
𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵𑍇 𑌮𑍇𑌷𑌗𑍇 𑌭𑌾𑌨𑍌 𑌮𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌥 𑌯𑌥𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌫𑌲𑌦𑍋 𑌭𑌵॥௧௦॥  
𑌯𑌥𑌾 𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵𑍋 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍋 𑌵𑌲𑍍𑌲𑌭𑍋 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑍇 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌦𑌃 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌹𑌾 𑌭𑌵॥௧௧॥  
---𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌾𑌲𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 ௯௫  
  
𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍇---  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌃---  
𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑍇𑌶 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌮𑍇𑌷𑌗𑍇 𑌰𑌵𑍌।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍁 𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵॥௩௩॥  
𑌅𑌰𑍍𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌃---  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌮𑍇𑌷𑌗𑍇 𑌭𑌾𑌨𑍌 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌯𑌣𑌃।  
𑌅𑌰𑍍𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌹𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑌾𑌣 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨॥௩௪॥  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌚 𑌹𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌯𑍇।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌣𑍀𑌤 𑌮𑌯𑌾 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌕𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍀𑌦𑌥॥௩௫॥  
𑌋𑌷𑌭𑌃 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌯𑌮𑌃 𑌸𑌮𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌨𑌃।  
𑌗𑍃𑌹𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑌯𑌾 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌯𑌥𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌫𑌲𑌦𑍋 𑌭𑌵॥௩௬॥  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌚𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌥 𑌪𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌚𑌰𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
---𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌵𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍇 ௪

6912385bd0.d: Magnitude: 17% of the solar diameter is covered (parimāṇa ≈2.0 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 01:04►14:36 (from 4 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra puṣyaḥ/āśrēṣā/maghā (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or jyēṣṭhā (anujanma) or rēvatī (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: karkaṭaḥ, siṁhaḥ, dhanuḥ, mēṣaḥ get more ashubha phala, vr̥śchikaḥ, makaraḥ, mīnaḥ, mithunam somewhat ashubha, kanyā, tulā, kumbhaḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.

696e8ce453.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°29′42.00″.
696e8ce453.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°29′42.00″, 0°29′22.11″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′57.35″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 3°59′23.42″ E). śukraḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°24′39.34″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 4°07′53.04″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

69c0d761a6.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in pūrvāṣāḍhā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°10′25.58″.
69c0d761a6.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°10′25.58″, 0°10′18.76″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°56′03.55″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 0°59′32.59″ E). śukraḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°45′37.97″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 0°49′52.33″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here aṅgārakaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

69e17f31ba.d: Kṛpāśaṅkara, son of Ātmasomayāji in Andhra in the lineage of Garga, with the name Gaṅgayya before initiation established six religions of worship in worshipping Śiva, Hari, Skanda and others away from Tantrik practices and establishing everywhere the non-dualism enunciated in the Vedas, drove away the notion of dualism. Kṛpāśaṅkara established Śrī Viśvarūpa at Śṛṅgeri under the directions of Śrī Kaivalya Munīndra and formulated precepts; having adorned Ācārya Pīṭha for forty-one years, he departed in the direction of Kubera, viz. North and attained siddhi at Vindhyas. The mighty omniscient (Kṛpāśaṅkara), the One without a second, attained the supreme non-dual state of the Ultimate known as parāpara which is full of Supreme Bliss on the third day of the dark fortnight in the month of Kārtika in the year Vibhava.

6a2c53726a.d: It is said in Vishnu Purāṇam that when Amavasya overlaps with one of nine nakshatras---Anuradha, Vishakha, Swati, Pushya, Ardra, Punarvasu, Shravishtha, Purvaproshthapada, or Shatabhishak---it is sacred even for Devas. For instance, Shraaddha done on an Amavasya joined with Anuradha, Vishakha, Swati keeps the pitrs satisfied for eight years. Likewise, on Pushya, Ardra and Punarvasu, the pitrs are satisfied for twelve years. It is said in the Smrtis, that if Amavasya falls on a Monday, Tuesday or Thursday, such a tithi is given the appellation puṣkalā and is as sacred as a solar eclipse. amāvāsyā of āśvayuja month.

एकैकेन तिलैर्मिश्रान् दद्यात् त्रींस्त्रीन् जलाञ्जलीन्।
संवत्सरकृतं पापं तत्क्षणादेव नश्यति॥

यत्र क्वचन नद्यां हि स्नात्वा कृष्णचतुर्दशीम्।
सन्तर्प्य धर्मराजं तु मुच्यते सर्वकिल्बिषैः॥
दक्षिणभिमुखो भूत्वा तिलैः सव्यं समाहितः।
देवतीर्थेन देवत्वात् तिलैः प्रेताधिपो यतः॥

6a3960c87b.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in uttaraprōṣṭhapadā mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°54′41.64″.
6a3960c87b.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°54′41.64″, 0°54′28.87″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°07′32.92″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.97, elongation 14°48′02.69″ E). śukraḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°12′51.28″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 14°41′59.35″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

6aa7ce90d2.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°41′09.75″, 0°41′02.39″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at śravaṇaḥ-4 makaraḥ (latitude 2°00′25.31″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.28, elongation 5°47′39.13″ E). śukraḥ at śravaṇaḥ-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°19′15.55″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 5°35′39.98″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

6aab1afd55.d: It is said in the Smrtis, that if Amavasya falls on a Monday, Tuesday or Thursday, such a tithi is given the appellation puṣkalā and is as sacred as a solar eclipse. amāvāsyā of the adhika jyaiṣṭha month.
6aab1afd55.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌸𑍋𑌮𑍇𑌨 𑌭𑍌𑌮𑍇𑌨 𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌣𑌾 𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾 𑌯𑌦𑌿।  
𑌸𑌾 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌕𑌲𑌾 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌣𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌭𑌾॥

6aad053c56.d:
On this day, Duch East India Company submitted to a peace treaty with mArtANDa varma of tirvanantapuram - abandoning all hopes of political and commercial dominance in keraLa, agreeing not to obstruct the Raja's expansion, and in turn, to sell to him arms and ammunition.

Context
In 1730s, mArtANDa varma started annexing and consolidating keraLa kingdoms. Dutch tried to stop him, but lost crucial battles. Some prominent dutch prisoners had switched to serving and upgrading mArtANDa varma's army.

6ae80cc931.b: Observed on Paurṇamāsī tithi of Phālgunaḥ (lunar) month (Aparāhṇaḥ/vyaapti).
6ae80cc931.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌯𑍋 𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃---  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌛𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍀 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌦𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚॥  
𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌆𑌷𑌾𑌢𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌦𑌶𑌮𑍀 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌷𑌾𑌢𑍀 𑌚 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌿𑌮𑌾।  
𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍀 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍀 𑌜𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍀 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾॥  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌃।  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁॥  
𑌹𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌦𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌆𑌸𑍁 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---   
𑌯𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌃।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌭𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌤𑌦𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌲𑌿𑌲𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌲𑌿𑌃।  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌹𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌬𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌃---

6b58b83077.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in puṣyaḥ karkaṭaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°33′10.65″.
6b58b83077.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°33′10.65″, 0°32′52.49″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at puṣyaḥ-4 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 0°29′56.97″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.79, elongation 12°31′32.54″ W). budhaḥ at puṣyaḥ-4 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 1°03′07.62″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.26, elongation 12°33′33.81″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

6b653cb25a.b: Observed on Paurṇamāsī tithi of Māghaḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
6b653cb25a.d: Last three days of māgha-māsaḥ are especially sacred. By means of baths in Māgha, calamities perish. By means of baths in Māgha sins perish. Māgha is superior to all sacrifices, and gives the fruit of (all kinds of) charity. Māgha roars (louder) than sacrifices. Māgha roars (louder) than yōga. And O vidyādhara, Māgha roars (louder) than severe penance. The fruit which men obtain by (observing) restraints for ten years at Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, Brahmāvarta having profuse water, at Avimukta, Prayāga, confluence of Gaṅgā and the ocean, is obtained by bathing for three days in Māgha! There is no doubt! Those, in whose mind there is, for a long time, interest in heaven, should bathe in water anywhere when the Sun is in makara. Those who desire to have qualities like (long) life, (good) health, wealth, handsomeness, good fortune, should not give up bathing in Māgha. So also those who are afraid of hell, of poverty that is heaped, should by all means bathe in the month of Māgha. O best king, for washing off the mud of poverty, sins and bad luck, there is no other remedy than a bath in Māgha. Acts done without faith give small fruits. (But) a bath in Māgha gives the entire fruit. He who, with or without a desire, bathes anywhere outside (his house) in water, does not have sorrows in this or in the next world. As in the two fortnights the Moon waxes and wanes, in the same way in Māgha sins decrease and the heap of religious merit increases. As various gems come up from a mine, so religious merit of men springs up due to a bath in Māgha. As the desire-yielding cow fulfils the desire, or the desire-yielding gem gives the desired object, so a bath in Māgha fulfils all desires in the world. Penance is the best in Kṛtayuga, knowledge in Tretā-yuga, sacrifice in Dvāpara, knowledge (devotion?) in Kaliyuga, and Māgha in all the ages. The bath in Māgha, O king, showers with the streams of merit all the varṇas and the stages of life. (Translation: https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-padma-purana/d/doc365704.html)
6b653cb25a.s:
𑌭𑍃𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌵𑌾𑌚---  
𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌶𑍋 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍈𑌰𑌘𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌃।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌕𑍋 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌃 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌫𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌃॥௬௭॥  
𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍋 𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌤𑌿 𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍇𑌭𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍋 𑌯𑍋𑌗𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌤𑌿।  
𑌤𑍀𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌚 𑌤𑌪𑌸𑍋 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍋 𑌭𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌧𑌰 𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌤𑌿॥௬௮॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌕𑌰𑍇 𑌚 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑍃𑌥𑍂𑌦𑌕𑍇।  
𑌅𑌵𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾𑌗𑍇 𑌚 𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌗𑌰𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌮𑍇॥௬௯॥  
𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌦𑌶𑌭𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌷𑍈𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌨𑌰𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨 𑌸𑌂𑌶𑌯𑌃॥௭௦॥  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌭𑍋𑌗𑍇 𑌚𑌿𑌰𑌂 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍋 𑌯𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌨𑌸𑌿 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌤𑍇।  
𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌕𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌜𑌲𑍇 𑌤𑍈𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑍃𑌗𑌭𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌰𑍇॥௭௧॥  
𑌆𑌯𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍋𑌗𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍌 𑌰𑍂𑌪𑍇 𑌸𑍁𑌭𑌗𑌤𑌾 𑌗𑍁𑌣𑍇।  
𑌯𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌨𑍋𑌰𑌥𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍈𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑍃𑌗𑌭𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌰𑍇॥   
𑌯𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌬𑌿𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿 𑌨𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌬𑍍𑌧𑍇𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌯𑍇।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌥𑌾 𑌤𑍈𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑍃𑌗𑌭𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌰𑍇॥௭௩॥  
𑌦𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌦𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌲𑌨𑌾𑌯 𑌵𑍈।  
𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨 𑌚𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌹𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌾𑌯𑌃 𑌸𑍁𑌰𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮॥௭௪॥   
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌹𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑌿 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌫𑌲𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌵𑍈।  
𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌦𑌦𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿॥௭௫॥  
𑌅𑌕𑌾𑌮𑍋 𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑌕𑌾𑌮𑍋 𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌕𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌬𑌹𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌲𑍇।  
𑌇𑌹𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌚 𑌦𑍁𑌃𑌖𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌯𑍀 𑌨 𑌪𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿॥௭௬॥  
𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍇 𑌯𑌥𑌾 𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍀𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑌥𑌾।

6b7e2f6a34.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śukraḥ in viśākhā tulā, center-to-center separation 0°59′15.11″.
6b7e2f6a34.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°59′15.11″, 0°59′05.44″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at viśākhā-3 tulā (latitude 1°53′50.04″ N, vakra (retrograde), magnitude +2.08, elongation 10°27′48.62″ W). śukraḥ at viśākhā-3 tulā (latitude 0°54′34.94″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.92, elongation 10°19′53.83″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

6bc79c1a72.d:
On this day, 21 synchronised bomb blasts took place within a span of few minutes in Ahmedabad - around 56 died, and 200 injured. Diabolically, 2 blasts took place inside the premises of two hospitals, about 40 minutes after the initial series of blasts. One of the blasts in the hospitals occurred when injured victims of the initial series of blasts were being admitted there. Several bombs were defused in the succeding hours.

Context
Carried out by Indian Mujahideen, an offshoot of Students Islamic Movement of India. In their email traced to Mumbai, they said: "In the name of Allah the Indian Mujahideen strike again! Do whatever you can, within 5 minutes from now, feel the terror of Death!”.

This came after May 13 Jaipur bombings (63 killed), 25 July bengaLUru bombings and was followed by Delhi bombings. 

            
Maulana Abdul Halim, a SIMI mastermind, was arrested a few days later. Several others were later arrested. In 2022, 38 Muslim terrorists were awarded death penalty, while 11 were given life imprisonment.

6bcce285b8.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°38′08.63″.
6bcce285b8.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°38′08.63″, 0°38′04.18″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at rēvatī-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 0°39′29.71″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.10, elongation 3°57′45.73″ W). budhaḥ at rēvatī-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°17′38.34″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.68, elongation 4°06′57.62″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

6c09906ec2.d:
Uttarāyaṇa-puṇyakālaḥ. For uttarāyaṇa, the 20 ghatikas succeeding the saṅkramaṇa form a puṇyakāla; in general, the ghatikas closer to the puṇyakāla are even more sacred.

While the nirayana puṇyakāla-s are well known, marked by the transit of the Sun into various rāśī-s (which confer the name to the corresponding saura month), there are also ayana-s and sāyana saṅkramaṇa-s, which mark the position of the Sun above the Northern or Southern parts of the Earth. These determine the r̥tu-s, and also the very famous uttarāyaṇa and dakṣināyana (movement of the Sun towards North or South, respectively). While these two types of puṇyakāla-s (sāyana and nirayana) coincided millennia ago, there has been a gradual precession of the equinoxes, owing to the nature of the Earth's rotation, causing the sāyana saṅkramaṇa-s to happen about 24 days before the nirayana saṅkramaṇa-s. In that era, uttarāyaṇa coincided with makara-saṅkramaṇa and dakṣināyana coincided with karkaṭaka-saṅkramaṇa, and the mēsa and tulā saṅkramaṇa-s corresponded to the equinoxes, when the Sun rises direct East (and sets direct West).

Many Dharma Shastra texts recognise the separate puṇyakāla-s for both types of saṅkramaṇa-s. The vachanam of Jaabaali Maharshi is mentioned above, where he says that the puṇyakāla-s are identical (in their reckoning) for both types of saṅkramaṇa-s. In Kala Madhava, which is considered as the source text of the kala vicharas of the Dikshitiya, it is said in the 5th prakarana that,  meṣādi-saṅkrāntayo yasmin dine bhavanti tasmād dināt pūrvebhyaḥ ekādaśabhyo dinebhyaḥ prācīne dine, noting that Sayana Sankramanas occurred ~11 days before the day when the Mesha Sankramanas etc occur. Further references are seen in Dharma Sindhu first pariccheda, Jayasimha Kalpadruma sankranti nirnaya and Nirnaya Sindhu first pariccheda. There are also ample references in Vedas, illustrating how Ayana-s happened much later (in certain other eras), e.g. Shukla Yajur Veda Shatapatha Brahmana (Ekapaat Kanda 1/2/3), Nakshatra Sukta belonging to the Atharva Veda (Shaunaka Samhita 19/7/2), Maitrayaniya Aranyaka (6/14), and Taittiriya Brahmana (1/5/2).

For a wonderfully detailed exposition on the topic, see https://sites.google.com/view/nakshatradarsha/dakshinayana-en and https://sites.google.com/view/nakshatradarsha/uttarayana-en .

6c1e771418.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śaniḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°33′48.24″.
6c1e771418.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°33′48.24″, 0°33′37.92″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°40′27.97″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.13, elongation 10°14′22.90″ W). śaniḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°14′16.21″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.70, elongation 10°20′43.94″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

6c36feafa2.b: Observed on Jyēṣṭhā nakshatra of Karkaṭaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
6c36feafa2.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Kotpuli Nayanmar, born in a Vellala family, was the Commander-in-Chief for a Chola king, and a devout follower of Bhagavan Shiva. He religiously bought paddy with his income to donate for Bhagavan's offerings in Shiva temples. Before leaving for a military assignment, he left a considerable amount of paddy, specifically designated for temple use, with his family. However, during a famine in his absence, his relatives, suffering from hunger, used this paddy for themselves. Upon returning and discovering this, the Nayanmar, deeply upset by their disregard for his instructions and their disrespect towards Bhagavan, killed them, including his own parents. His devotion to Bhagavan Shiva surpassed even his familial bonds. In response, Bhagavan Shiva appeared to the Nayanmar, blessing him and granting salvation to him and all the relatives who perished by his hand.

6c42a84c0c.d:
The Shukla-paksha Ekadashi of māgha month is known as bhaimī-ēkādaśī. If this coincides with the nakshatram Punarvasu, the tithi is even more special and is known by the appellation jayā.

The fruits of fasting on Ekādaśī are greatly extolled in the Padma Purana—

A person who bathes at Śaṃkhoddhāra and beholds the image of Viṣṇu does not acquire even a sixteenth of the merit earned by fasting on Ekādaśī. O noble king, even if one gives four lakhs of coins on the days of the Sun's transition between Zodiac signs, it does not equal even a sixteenth of the merit from an Ekādaśī fast! Indeed, fasting on Ekādaśī grants the same religious merit as bathing at Prabhāsa during a lunar or solar eclipse. One who drinks the sacred water at Kedāra is freed from rebirth, and likewise, fasting on Ekādaśī removes the cycle of rebirth.

The merit from an Ekādaśī fast is a hundred times greater than the reward of performing an Ashvamedha sacrifice on earth. Fasting on Ekādaśī yields a hundredfold more merit than gifting a thousand cows to a learned brāhmaṇa. Those who fast on Ekādaśī are considered equal to those whose bodies are inhabited by Brahma, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The merit from observing the Ekādaśī vow is immeasurable, and difficult to obtain even by the Devas. There is no other vow like that of the Ekādaśī, that destroys sins.

𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑌾 𑌋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍁𑌃।  
𑌨𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌨𑌾 𑌸𑌾 𑌚 𑌜𑌯𑌾 𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌾 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌾 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌃।
